comparator.name: Applied Mathematics
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations prescribe a 165 EC major and 15 EC minor in the standard route. This example uses the Applied Mathematics first-year project, the first two listed choices in each upper-year group and Statistical Modelling as the remaining elective.
components: The Applied Mathematics project is one of two first-year choices. Students draw on first-year mathematics to investigate an applied problem.
Differential Equations in Science and Engineering
One of the two required modelling or systems project choices illustrated here. Uses earlier differential equations, numerical methods and scientific computing.
The second project choice illustrated here. Builds on first-year Linear Systems.
One of two advanced choices illustrated here. Uses earlier linear algebra and numerical analysis, including Python.
The other advanced choice illustrated here. Builds on Linear Algebra 1 and 2 and Linear Systems.
Mathematics & Society: Ethical and Professional Aspects
The example uses Statistical Modelling as the elective. It builds on Probability Theory and Statistics.
Builds on the first-year project and second-year mathematics and must be completed before the bachelor’s project.
Requires completion of year one and 150 EC in the degree, including project preparation, with an approved study programme and career portfolio. Students must also enrol in the project.
The standard route includes 15 EC of minor space. The courses depend on the minor chosen.

core: Applied mathematical modelling, numerical mathematics, systems and control, optimisation, proofs, calculus, linear algebra, probability and differential equations
Scientific programming, computational simulation, algorithms and data-based modelling
Translating real systems into tractable quantitative models and evaluating assumptions and solutions
adjacent: Mathematics in engineering, physics, Earth and sustainable technological systems
Mathematical and computational models of living and biomedical systems
questions: How can mathematical, numerical and computational models describe, predict and optimise complex systems?
How can quantitative models be applied honestly to technological, physical and biological problems?

Connects wave observations, chemical analysis and materials properties to sustainability questions.
Prepares, joins and visualizes tabular, text and spatial data in R, including a project using data from a field of interest.

studies numerical image processing, feature detection and tracking for technological applications without claiming optical instrumentation

develops probability, estimation and simulation for uncertain measurements and model parameters

extends calculus to multiple dimensions, complex functions and differential equations for natural and technological systems

examines recycling, recovery and remediation technologies, resource security, materials and laboratory work for circular technological systems
conducts advanced research on geothermal energy, carbon storage, waste storage and resource constraints

develops epidemiological reasoning and critical evaluation of health evidence for medical-technology contexts
introduces brain–behaviour relationships and neuroscience foundations for living-system models
studies neural structure and function using comparative, microscopic and ethical perspectives
develops biomolecular and metabolic foundations for modelling living systems
studies cellular organisation and molecular mechanisms relevant to biological technologies
connects anatomy, function and imaging in the study of human systems
examines physical and chemical processes that sustain integrated human physiology
studies genetic, inflammatory and tissue-repair mechanisms in disease
Investigates attention, memory and cognitive control through experimental evidence and research design.
Uses biochemical, microbial and molecular protocols and introductory bioinformatics to interpret and document laboratory results.
Connects immune mechanisms to infection and disease and analyses original flow-cytometry data.
integrates cellular defects, disease mechanisms, clinical cases and treatment reasoning
Uses quantitative estimates, simulation and mini-grid work to assess energy supply, storage and demand.

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, algorithms & autonomous systems
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by mathematics, programming, algorithms, data, optimisation, linear systems, machine learning and robotics, with a smaller sustainable-technology application strand. The label does not claim proof-based analysis, topology, functional analysis, partial differential equations or Applied Mathematics project formation.
alternatives.concept: Study how mathematical models and algorithms describe and control systems. Combine calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods and signals with machine learning, robot motion and decisions under uncertainty.
progression: Programming precedes algorithm design and intelligent systems. Mathematical Methods leads into linear algebra and numerical methods, and linear algebra supports Robotics. Machine Learning precedes neural networks.

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, Earth systems & sustainable technology
alternatives.labelReason: Modelling and computation support a sustained Earth and energy sequence, from system modelling and field evidence to geochemistry, recovery and energy design.
alternatives.concept: Use mathematical models and field and laboratory evidence to study Earth and energy systems. Explore climate and geochemistry, measure properties of soils and aquifers, and assess renewable energy and resource recovery.
progression: Sustainability Essentials I prepares for Earth-system modelling and Sustainability Essentials II. Energy & Sustainability and Sustainability Essentials II precede Renewable System Design. Data analysis precedes statistical learning.
alternatives.distinctness: 7 courses (52.5 EC) differ in each direction. Earth-system modelling, geophysics, geochemistry, materials recovery and renewable-energy assessment replace specialist computing and autonomous-system courses.
traceOverrides: supplies programming, testing and debugging for implementing mathematical and natural-system models
develops logic and discrete structures for computational modelling
develops data preparation, visualisation and manipulation for scientific investigations
implements regression and statistical-learning methods for modelled natural systems
studies numerical image processing, feature detection and tracking for quantitative observation
develops neural-network and deep-learning models for advanced scientific data analysis

alternatives.label: Quantitative bioscience, imaging & computational modelling
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum contains a sustained molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease-science core alongside mathematics, programming, imaging and data modelling. It does not claim mathematical biology, biophysics or Applied Mathematics equivalence.
alternatives.concept: Combine mathematics and computing with the study of living systems. Use statistical learning and image analysis alongside molecular biology, anatomy, physiology and laboratory work.
progression: Cellular and molecular foundations lead to biochemistry, anatomy, physiology and laboratory work. Programming precedes computer vision, and data analysis and statistical learning precede neural networks. Brain and behaviour prepares for advanced cognition.
alternatives.distinctness: 97.5 EC differ from the autonomous-systems option and 97.5 EC differ from the Earth and energy option, in each direction. The biomedical option combines a quantitative core with molecular, anatomical, laboratory and health science.
traceOverrides: supplies programming, testing and debugging for quantitative biomedical models
develops data preparation and visualisation for biomedical and health investigations
implements regression and statistical-learning methods for biological and clinical data
studies numerical image processing, feature detection and tracking relevant to medical imaging without claiming physical instrumentation
develops neural-network and deep-learning models for advanced biomedical data and image analysis

candidates.label: Engineering, physical systems and sustainable technology

selection.assessment: Three distinct options share a quantitative foundation. The closest option focuses on mathematical and computational models of autonomous systems. The other options apply quantitative methods to Earth and energy systems or to bioscience and health.

blocks: Both use programming to solve problems. Groningen builds directly on calculus and linear algebra in scientific programming.
Both use logic, sets and proof. Groningen continues this foundation into proof-based analysis.
Both introduce differentiation and integration. UCR also uses complex numbers and differential equations in a dynamic modelling project.
Both address optimisation; UCR focuses on search and constraint-satisfaction methods for AI rather than a full applied-mathematics optimisation course.
Both directly study systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces; Groningen continues to a second dedicated linear-algebra course.
Both study numerical integration, interpolation and equation solving. UCR tests accuracy and stability using Mathematica, while Groningen uses Python.
Both use differential equations to analyse linear systems. UCR emphasizes signals, transforms and feedback. Groningen continues into advanced systems theory.
Both establish probability concepts and distributions; UCR combines probability with statistical inference and simulation.
Both develop statistical models; UCR teaches regression, classification and machine-learning methods rather than Groningen's dedicated Statistical Modelling elective.
Both extend calculus to several variables. UCR also introduces complex-valued functions and differential equations.
Both construct and evaluate models of complex systems; UCR does so specifically for interacting Earth systems rather than as a general applied-mathematics modelling course.
Groningen requires a 15 EC project in Applied Mathematics. UCR’s optional independent research is listed separately and depends on the topic and available supervision.

notes.text: The UCR options share methods in calculus, numerical computing, linear systems and modelling. Groningen requires a deeper sequence in proof-based analysis, topology, differential equations and systems theory, along with staged mathematical projects and a dedicated bachelor’s project.

audience.programmeDescription: Applied Mathematics at the University of Groningen combines mathematical proof with modelling and computation. Students develop methods for analysing systems, solve problems from science and engineering, and complete an applied mathematics research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related study in mathematical modelling and autonomous systems, Earth and energy systems, or quantitative bioscience. Groningen develops greater depth in mathematical proof, analysis, differential equations and systems theory.
